https://www.planetf1.com/f1-data/kimi-an.text: Kimi Antonelli penalty: Was it deserved? Kimi Antonelli ’s three-place grid penalty for failing to slow sufficiently under yellow flags has reignited questions over how the FIA judges these incidents, with telemetry suggesting his Hungary case was remarkably similar to George Russell’s escape in Austria. Exactly how much Kimi slowed down, how much time it cost him, and how this situation compares to Austria where Russell avoided a penalty, we analyse with the help of telemetry data. Kimi Antonelli telemetry analysis explains Hungarian GP yellow flag penalty During his final flying lap in Q3, Kimi Antonelli encountered yellow flags in the last corner of the track due to Max Verstappen going off. As the rules state, under a single yellow flag situation, drivers must slow down sufficiently to make their passage through that section of the track safe. But exactly how much isn’t clearly defined, leaving it to the stewards to make a decision. In the end, Kimi improved his time, putting him in fourth position behind Norris and both Ferrari drivers. We had an almost identical situation in Austria, when Max Verstappen going off track brought out yellow flags. Back then, Antonelli aborted his lap completely, whereas Russell, in the stewards’ opinion, slowed down enough to secure pole position and, later, the victory. It was a good lesson for the young Italian who, judging by the stewards’ ruling, still hasn’t learned it. By analysing the two flying laps Kimi set during Q3 in Hungary (with the white line representing Kimi’s second attempt), we can see exactly how much he slowed down. The biggest difference can be seen in throttle application – upon seeing the yellow flags, Kimi lifted off the throttle pedal about 30 metres earlier. This affected his maximum speed before braking, which was 6km/h lower than on his previous lap. Once he passed Verstappen, the track was green, allowing him to get back to a full push. But despite that, Antonelli applied the throttle about 35 metres later. Naturally, this impacted his exit speed as well as his lap time all the way to the line. Only in the final few metres of the lap did Antonelli return to his typical speed for that part of the circuit. We can also see a fairly clear difference on the graph in brake pedal application. But how much time did this cost Antonelli? Before encountering the yellow flags, Kimi had a negative delta time of 0.156 seconds compared to his first Q3 attempt – in other words, up to that point he was 0.156 seconds faster. In the end, this delta time was 0.100 seconds, meaning he lost approximately 0.05 to 0.06 seconds due to Verstappen’s incident. According to the stewards, this wasn’t enough, so Kimi was handed a 3-place grid penalty , dropping him to P7. In comparison with the situation in Austria, Russell’s numbers looked like this: Russell lifted off the throttle pedal about 100 metres earlier than on the previous lap; however, his re-application of the throttle after passing Verstappen showed no difference. He lost about 0.08 seconds compared to his previous lap, and the stewards deemed his lap entirely legal. Can we say that between a deceleration worth 0.08 seconds and one worth 0.05 seconds lies the threshold for deciding whether a driver slowed down safely enough? In my opinion, no – both cases are far too similar for the outcome to differ like this. This penalty will heavily impact Antonelli’s race, with the Mercedes driver likely out of podium contention before the lights have even gone out. https://albaniandailynews.com/news/spain.text: Home Politics Economy Current Events Op-Ed Social Sport Region World News Contact Share Tweet Spain Imposes Border Controls Against Italy as Row Over Ceuta Migrant Influx Intensifies Current Event Saturday, August 8, 2026 Spain has imposed border controls on all air and sea travel from Italy as a row between the two EU countries intensifies. The measures - which started at midnight (22:00 GMT) and will last for a month - come a week after Italy introduced similar restrictions following an influx of about 78,000 migrants from Morocco into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta. Spanish officials said the documents of 5%-10% of passengers were being checked before they were allowed to disembark planes. Italy has also said its border controls are random. The crisis has pitted Spain's socialist leader Pedro Sanchez against Italy's conservative leader Giorgia Meloni - who has long called for stricter EU migration rules. Italy does not share a land border with Spain. Its government said last week that decision to temporarily suspend the ?border-free Schengen arrangement was to prevent any of the migrants who had entered Ceuta from travelling on to Italy. Madrid dismissed this position, saying it was based on "spurious arguments" that lacked any basis in fact because the migrants who entered Ceuta had no way of entering the Schengen area. On Friday, Spain demanded Italy reverse its checks by Sunday. Rome said they would stay until at least 15 August - when, it said, Spain "expects a new wave of migration" to hit Ceuta. Italy has said that Spanish and EU citizens are exempt from additional checks when arriving in Italy, with these extra steps only for non-EU residents. However, it is not clear how border officials were meant to distinguish between EU and non-EU travellers and El Pais has reported that several Italian airport terminals have seen long queues and waiting times in recent days, with passengers arriving from Spain directed to a specific line for checks. As for Spanish controls, the authorities insists the immigration checks are random. However, a passenger arriving in Madrid on Saturday told national broadcaster RTVE that all passengers on her flight had had to show their passports. "They told us we couldn't get off the plane without showing our documents," Elisa said. Another passenger said "we were stopped and asked for identification, which the police seemed to approve of". Spain says its checks will stay in place until 7 September "unless a change in the circumstances that led to its adoption warrants modifying that period". Temporary suspensions of the Schengen agreement are not unprecedented. Italy also maintains controls on its border with Slovenia. Italy's decision to suspend Schengen for a month was backed by Finland and Denmark, while the Czech Republic called for Spain's membership to be temporarily suspended. Most of the migrants who arrived in Ceuta last week were returned within days. One hundred are believed to have died during the crossing. Nearly 1,400 minors, some of them "very young boys and girls", still remain there. Spain has not announced an anticipated second wave of crossings from Morocco. But BBC Arabic has found dozens of Facebook posts calling for a second crossing in mid-August, including some that advertised swimming equipment for sale. Six of these groups had more than 100,000 followers. Meta says it has removed posts that violate its policy. The Spanish prime minister's office told El Pais they were monitoring the situation but did not expect a repeat of scenes from last week. It remains unclear exactly why tens of thousands of migrants attempted to cross into Ceuta, but the EU's Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner has suggested criminal networks spreading disinformation were to blame - an assertion the Spanish government has agreed with. The crossings came after Spain's Supreme Court ruled that migrants stopped at sea while trying to reach Ceuta or Melilla cannot be summarily returned to Morocco. Morocco, for its part, has laid blame for the crisis on the court, with an unnamed government source briefing local outlets that "the deterrent element of the system collapsed and the dam gave way, not under the weight of the criminals, but of a judge's decision". The number of people swimming to Ceuta at once has raised questions about why Morocco's border guards did not attempt to stop them. The two exclaves have long been a bone of diplomatic contention between Spain and Morocco, which does not recognise Spanish sovereignty over them. Photograph: Tom Lartige Catillon/Getty Images Protest ‘A powerful warning’: will Europe’s angry protests lead to real political change? Hamstrung governments seem to have no answer to the public’s furious demands, making further discontent likely Europe live – latest updates Ashifa Kassam European community affairs correspondent Wed 21 Oct 2026 05.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google I n France , it was the piles of wheelie bins stacked up against school entrances that first hinted at the scale of student anger over crumbling classrooms and teacher shortages. In Spain, it was a tent camp that steadily grew in the heart of the capital as residents railed against soaring housing costs. Similar scenes have since sprung up in Belgium, Italy and Portugal , and clashes have convulsed Albania’s capital of Tirana, hinting at an autumn of protests across Europe. Much of the news coverage in recent days has focused on the violence that played out on the fringes of the protests in France and Italy . The protests themselves, however, point to what seems to be a diverse response to a common crisis: the growing perception, particularly among younger generations, that governments are unable, or unwilling, to deliver when it comes to affordable housing, social equality and robust public services. graphic “This is the most powerful warning from Europe’s angry youth today, in France and across the continent,” the policy analyst Alberto Alemanno said. The framing stands in sharp contrast to the many rightwing and far-right voices who have sought to exploit the violence in France and Italy, linking it without evidence to migration while brushing over protesters’ wider demands. Officials in France have dismissed any link between the violence and immigration. The country’s president, Emmanuel Macron, said on Sunday that the “unbridled violence” had been carried out by French people. 10:46 France protests escalate with riots, looting and 2,400 arrests - The Latest Alemanno, a professor of EU law at the HEC business school in Paris, said he had received an unprecedented number of calls from right-wing, xenophobic outlets in recent days, many of them seeking to fuel the idea of the protests as some sort of “pan-European revolt”. It is a narrative that he describes as misleading. “The demonstrations have different causes and do not necessarily share political objectives,” he wrote this week . “Yet their rapid spread hints at a common weak point: too many young Europeans doubt that existing institutions can deliver the security, opportunity and voice they expect.” The head of the Paris office of the European Council on Foreign Relations, Célia Belin, said some of those doubts were currently being reinforced in France. “Faced with the high discontent of young people in high school, the government has no answer for them,” she said, citing an administration squeezed financially by a high deficit and debt-to-GDP ratio and limited politically by the country’s deadlocked parliament. “Basically the answer is: ‘There’s no money, there is nothing we can do.’ And that’s a huge problem.” graphic The view echoes that of the secretary general of France’s CGT union, Sophie Binet, after Saturday’s protests in which about half a million people turned up to rail against the rising cost of living and deteriorating public services. Binet condemned the violence, but she noted that the government had little choice when it came to quelling the protests. “Today’s mobilisation confirms the depth of the anger,” she said. “To get out of the crisis, there is only one way. Respond to the demands.” Albania has also been shaken by mass student demonstrations for the past week after protests initially prompted by a proposal to build a resort backed by Donald Trump’s family. In Milan, people took to the streets to protest against the rising cost of living, giving voice to the deep inequalities that now course through a city where an estimated one in 12 people is reportedly a millionaire . skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion graphic In Lisbon’s Rossio Square, housing campaigners set up camp on Saturday surrounded by banners that read “homeless generation” and “I just want a home to live in” and vowing to stay on as long as possible. It was an echo of the protests that have sprung up in Porto in recent weeks as residents push back against housing prices that more than doubled between 2015 and 2024, rising roughly twice as fast as the EU average. The managing director for Europe at the consulting firm Eurasia Group, Mujtaba Rahman, said what had burst into public view was not a single, coordinated European movement. Instead the events of recent days had laid bare a “convergence of distinct national protest movements”, each with substantially different triggers. View image in fullscreen Protesters camp out in Lisbon’s Rossio Square. Photograph: Horacio Villalobos/Corbis/Getty Images “What links them is a growing perception that European governments are unable to deliver affordable housing, functioning public services and economic security, particularly for younger generations,” he said, citing a growing gap between public expectations and governments’ fiscal capacity. “This mismatch between political demands and economic reality is likely to remain and grow over time, which suggests further discontent and protests are likely over the medium term,” he said. Arancha González, the dean of the Paris School of International Affairs and a former Spanish foreign minister, went a step further when asked this month about the similarities between the housing protests in Spain and the school protests in France. “The reasons are different, but they share the same spark: the breakdown of the social contract,” she told the Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera. “Young French people are protesting for education, young Spanish people for housing, but in Europe, the idea that economies generate wellbeing and social equality has been shattered.” In Portugal, the campers were dislodged on Tuesday, leading to a fresh call for more housing protests. Similar calls for protests in the coming days have been heard across France, Spain and Italy, hinting at the tremendous task that lies ahead for officials across Europe, said Alemanno. “They must protect peaceful demonstrators, hold those responsible for criminal acts accountable, and address the underlying pressures, from housing costs and insecure work to strained public services and an uncertain technological future,” he said. “Europe’s democratic institutions will be judged not by how forcefully they condemn disorder, but by whether they can turn generational anger into tangible political change.” Explore more on these topics Protest France Italy Portugal Spain Albania Europe features Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development
